paragraphs: Three sheep on a farm in County Down have a disease called bluetongue. Agriculture Minister Andrew Muir gave the news on 13 November. These are the first cases in Northern Ireland this winter.
Small flies called midges spread the virus. They bite animals. Cows, sheep, goats, deer, llamas and alpacas can get sick. People cannot get it. Milk and meat are safe to eat.
The virus was already found in Northern Ireland in November 2025. So there will be no new rules on moving animals, said chief vet Brian Dooher.
Officials will keep checking animals. Farmers should tell them about sick animals. Cold weather means fewer midges. The disease was also found in Britain and the Republic this year.

農業部長安德魯．繆爾在11月13日公布了這個消息。
這是北愛爾蘭今年冬天的首批病例。

paragraphs: Bluetongue virus has been found in three sheep on a farm in County Down. Northern Ireland's Agriculture Minister, Andrew Muir, announced the news on 13 November. These are the first cases in Northern Ireland this winter.

The virus, called BTV-3, is spread by small biting insects known as midges. It can make cattle, sheep, goats, deer, llamas and alpacas ill. However, it is an animal disease. Muir said it is not a danger to people, and milk and meat are still safe to eat.

The Chief Veterinary Officer, Brian Dooher, explained that the virus was already confirmed in Northern Ireland in November 2025. Because of this, there will be no new limits on moving animals and no new control zones.
The agriculture department, Daera, will continue to test animals at abattoirs and animals brought in from other EU countries. Farmers are asked to report any animals they think are sick.

Diana Armstrong, who leads the Assembly's agriculture committee, said the news was not a surprise. She added that colder weather means midges are less active. This year, cases have also been found in Great Britain and in the Republic, including a herd of cattle in County Wexford in September.

paragraphs: Northern Ireland has recorded its first outbreak of bluetongue this winter, after the BTV-3 strain of the virus was identified in three sheep on a County Down holding. The Agriculture Minister, Andrew Muir, disclosed the findings on 13 November, marking the opening cases of the 2026/27 season.

Carried by biting midges, the virus can strike a broad range of ruminants and camelids, including cattle, sheep, goats, deer, llamas and alpacas. Muir was quick to reassure the public that the disease poses no risk to humans and has no bearing on food safety, meaning milk and meat can be consumed as normal.

According to the Chief Veterinary Officer, Brian Dooher, the virus had already gained a foothold in Northern Ireland when it was confirmed in November 2025. As a result, officials see no grounds for imposing fresh movement restrictions or disease control zones.

Daera, the agriculture department, is nonetheless keeping a close watch, carrying out active surveillance at abattoirs and screening susceptible livestock imported from mainland EU states. Farmers have been called upon to flag any suspected cases promptly.

Diana Armstrong, chair of the Assembly's agriculture committee, remarked that the news hardly came as a surprise, pointing out that falling temperatures curb midge activity. The disease has likewise surfaced in Great Britain and the Republic this year, with a cattle herd in County Wexford affected in September.
